Now, the other document counsel for the Defence showed you was this Cesko document, a letter written to the Defence by Cesko and this is in respect to inquiries by learned Defence counsel. And this was in regard of whether Halilovic gave an order to you to take Cesko trench-digging and all the other things that happened. Now, do you remember that order or would you like to see -- do you remember that letter or would you like to see it again? Because a question I would like to ask you in respect of that particular letter is this: Is there anything in the letter to suggest that Halilovic did not give such an order?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, at the time what people were saying, this Cesko was a handsome man, if you like, in some way. And at the time what people were saying was that he was having an affair of some sorts with Mrs. Dika. I think that was the most important reason why Sefer Halilovic had issued an order for this man to be taken trench-digging. He wasn't standing in his way otherwise. He had a private business throughout the war, and even if he was mobilised at one point, it's not something that I'm aware of. I know he was never sent to any of the front lines. But that was the reason usually given for the fact that Sefer Halilovic had issued an order for him to be taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And would this be an oral order or a written order, just to be quite clear again, of course?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an oral order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't intend to be very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The other thing you were asked by learned counsel for the Defence were that -- this is in respect of the ethnic composition of your brigade, the 9th Motorised Brigade, and you said to the question that soldiers were good people and it was a multi-ethnic unit, this was the proposition put to you and you got along together to the extent -- there was tolerance and friendship among the Serbs, Croats, and Muslim soldiers. You said in response to that question: "To the extent it was possible." Now, I was wondering whether you would like to elaborate on what you meant, "to the extent it was possible."

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time in Sarajevo, there were many people getting killed because of the shelling and there were many children getting killed all the time, civilians in general. There was a concern that - what shall I call it? - there could be an execution or massacre of these soldiers. Usually when you have a crime happening, you're probably familiar with the various types of crimes against civilians that occurred as a result of the shelling. There was a concern felt by the brigade that there would be revenge against these soldiers because sometimes the soldiers' brothers or children were among those who were killed; that's why great care was taken to prevent the revenge killings. The reason was that there was a large number of Serbs who remained in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you -- do you have any examples yourself when there were what you just referred to as "revenge killings"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be -- excuse me. It should be made clear whether my friend is talking about within the 9th Brigade or including other brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this question should be confined to in the 9th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In the 9th Brigade, your brigade.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were attempts which were foiled. There were cases where family members of our soldiers were among those who were killed. In the area of responsibility of the 9th Motorised Brigade there were attempts to execute some people; however, all these attempts were foiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, I was distracted for a minute, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the other question that you were asked by learned counsel for the Defence was as to where Sefer Halilovic was before the soldiers set off -- the unit chosen set off to Herzegovina, and you replied to his question as to where was Sefer at that time. You said: "Sefer went there before to carry out the preparations down there." Now, could you try to assist the Judges as to what kind of preparations would a commander undertake in the theatre of future combat activity before a military operation such as Neretva 93?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that didn't arise out of cross-examination. The question there concerns something quite different, which was: Where was Sefer Halilovic? Not what he was doing. And it's too late to be asking what a commander might get up to on the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that will be a very big question for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can limit it to what he thought Sefer Halilovic -- what preparations Sefer Halilovic was making. It does arise from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask about the location where Mr. Halilovic was at that time, because if you ask about the whole preparations for a campaign, for a military action, that is a big question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I stand guided by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know where Sefer Halilovic was as you went, as you said, making preparations for the operation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have been at Jablanica. Because of the comprehensive nature and the sheer size of the operation, he had to be at Jablanica. Before the units left Sarajevo, this applies particularly to that area, the Neretva River valley, I don't believe that anyone else could have made contact with those units, save for Sefer Halilovic. It was on account of the comprehensive nature of the job in the area that he simply had to be there, that and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Delalic for that. I'd like now to take you to the one final area and I'd like to give you an opportunity to comment on this. You have been cross-examined at some length on your 2nd December interview to the Sarajevo cantonal court to Ibrahim Hadzic. And there have been several contradictions or apparent contradictions pointed out to you. Now, Mr. Delalic, one of the reasons you put forward to the Your Honours was the reason why there are these contradictions, that these were not your words but they were of the judge himself. And one reason you said was because you had quarrelled with the judge. I'd like you please to assist you -- Their Honours by telling us the nature of this quarrel and were there any other reasons? And this is your opportunity to tell Their Honours why it was so.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after I appeared in court and I had been brought in by the police early in the morning, I had been asleep at home, the police came to take me away. Brought me to the court building. I was made to stay in the room for about one or two hours. And at the very outset I was becoming fidgety. This was not the usual practice. There should have been a summons or something like that to call me to appear before this tribunal, but there was none of that. So the first thing that angered me when I arrived in the court building, I had a right to be legally represented by counsel. But my counsel who is present here today was busy elsewhere on a different job and I requested to have a reprieve of several hours until my counsel was available or perhaps to postpone the interview for an entire day. I was not willing to provide any statements in the absence of my lawyer. This was refused. And although I was entitled to have my counsel beside me, he started taking a statement from me, having ordered the typist to start with my personal information. I opposed this. I refused to talk about it until I had a lawyer present. I had asked him previously whether I was entitled to this, to legal representation, and he said that I was. But since my lawyer was not there, we could just continue our interview. I wasn't familiar enough with the law and I believe that he was right and that indeed he was entitled to start the interview. So I started telling him about certain events in relation to Grabovica. I'm not sure the interpreter is catching up. The judge did not understand what the word "hierarchy" meant in a military context. So that was the first thing we clashed over. What was recorded was a different thing altogether and then -- there were two concepts being used, hierarchy and resubordination and our clash was about these two concepts. He simply didn't know what the word "resubordination" meant; he wasn't familiar with the concept. It wasn't part of his language. So he recorded an entire sentence that I didn't like and something that I didn't say to begin with, something about resubordinating my unit to Zulfikar Alispago, and the way he had it recorded in the transcript was entirely different. I tried to explain to him what the word "resubordination" meant. He attacked me, telling me that I -- he would not stand to be taught by me how to do his job. I asked him to change this word, "resubordination," and some other sentences, too, but he refused and we clashed and we started arguing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But you signed, nevertheless, the statement?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was supposed to under the law. I had to give this statement; there's no doubt about that. However, it was about the manner in which he wanted this statement taken, and I refused to agree. I asked for the interview to be postponed again, to be delayed, and I asked to have my lawyer present, but he refused. So I continued giving my statement. And at one point I asked not to provide these explanations to him, but rather that the typist should write down verbatim what I was saying, word-for-word, and not through the judge, because how it worked is I gave a statement to the judge and the judge would repeat this for the benefit of the typist. So what I asked to be done is for the typist to record my words, not the judge's words. So an argument ensued, and after the whole thing was over, my lawyer arrived and by way of demonstration I signed the statement. I didn't slam the door, because they allege that I had smashed the door, which wasn't true. I just fled the room. But the statement was never completed. Which judge was it? You'll probably want to know. This judge did not meet the requirements that were later applied in order to be re-elected as a judge. This man is nothing now. He's selling candy on the streets of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, I was actually referring to the Ibrahim, whatever his name is, Hadzic's judgement. Are you talking about somebody else now? What you've just said about this judge as selling candy on the streets. We just want the record to be clear. Are you talking about another judge or are you talking about Ibrahim, this last sentence you just said?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about this judge who heard me on that occasion. I think it was Ibrahim Hadzic. He took my statement on Grabovica when I gave this statement before the cantonal or municipal court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge El Mahdi, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, in your reply you stated, and I will quote you: "I did prepare a letter, needless to say," end of quote. This related to the time before you came to this Tribunal to testify. So I wonder how you prepared yourself. Do you have any memos, do you have any notes or things you had drafted at the time we are interested in?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DELALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I am glad you're asking me this. I didn't say that I had written a letter; I said that in some way I had to prepare because I believe that once I appeared before this Tribunal -- or rather, I believed that the investigators of this Tribunal were already in possession of everything that one needed to know about these incidents. I am absolutely convinced that no one would stand a chance lying before this Tribunal. A lot of these documents were mislaid and a lot of these documents were handed over by me to the investigators. A lot of the documents were taken away from me. I tried to prepare myself in order not to contradict myself. I value this Tribunal and hold it in very high esteem. I did not want to end up giving untruthful testimony before this Tribunal, and that's why I needed to prepare in some way. Before each of the statements I gave, I would talk about the gist of what went on. But now, I really had to prepare because it was suggested to me that details would be discussed before this Trial Chamber. So in a way I tried to prepare myself. I tried to make the bits and pieces stick, so as not to be confused once I had to render my version of events. I wanted to make sure that I would be honest and forthright in giving my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of the Judge's question? It seems none. At this stage are there any documents to tender? From the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We have some. MFI 415 and MFI 419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've just looked -- I've just lost my note of what those were. One of them is the tape, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- maybe since we are sitting here for a week, so it's very difficult to trace those documents at this moment. So maybe we could defer the admission of documents until a later stage. And the Prosecution's tendering documents is on the table, and I hope the Defence, which is more confusing to me, should submit us with a list as well as to the Prosecution. Maybe next Monday we could come back to visit this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, could I just for the record indicate the ones that there are. There's MFI 420, the Hadzic judgement; the Zadro statements admitted; 422 is Dani article; 423, the Vildana Selimbegovic letter; 414, the Cesko letter; 425, the letter from Omerbegovic; 426, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll return to 426, the Dahic judgement; 427, this witness's own judgement in 1994; and MFI 428, the letter from Mr. Baltic. Can I indicate I'm going to consider the matter of the letter from Mr. Baltic, it was obtained in haste and the learned Prosecutor has pointed out an error in terms of that so that we need to clarify whether the witness has -- whether Mr. Baltic has made an error as to which brigade he is talking about or whether in fact he is talking about the 9th Mountain Brigade which was a unit within the 1st Corps, although that was based outside. So we will consult about that and we will be ready to respond on Monday morning, if that is suitable as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So I think the same rule also applies to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I make it quite easy for the Defence counsel so they know my view on the matter. I would object to all the other documents but not the letters from potential witnesses. But the others I have no objection to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So you mean you object to document 428, but as to the others, there's no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, and the Cesko, the Cesko -- all the three letters, Your Honour, which have come have witnesses, the Cesko and this Sadika --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think -- so 424, 425, and 428?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, those are the three letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Cesko, Omerbegovic, and Baltic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So I believe I could make a decision at this moment. The other documents are admitted into the evidence. The three letters are still pending there until Monday. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence, and we really wish you a very pleasant trip back home. When we adjourn, Madam Usher will show you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank the Trial Chamber for hearing me out, and I wish you every success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The last matter, that is the proofing notes for the next witness. It seems to me that it is impossible for the Prosecution to furnish that proofing notes a little bit earlier. So we'll ask the court deputy to look territory possibility if that we could sit in the afternoon on Monday so that the Defence could have the whole morning, the whole period of morning, to prepare their case. But I hope that the parties will get informed about this possibility in a timely fashion. So I wish everybody a pleasant weekend. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of May, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
